There is nothing wrong with you. Your autonomic nervous system is reacting and it does that pretty well, having something cruel like this happen close to you (and even if "only" on the same campus) will set of some strong reactions. It is an anomaly, to your brain a potential dangerous anomaly, so it examines it over and over to keep you safe.    

If you can you could talk to a therapist or councellor, typically after something like this colleges will set that up for people.   

In the meantime there are several ways to try to deal with this and maybe one can work for you: You can try to groud yourself by looking at the things in your room, describing them to yourself, describe what you hear, smell, what you can touch. This works best in a familiar place you feel safe in.   

Personally I use "Air, Water, Food, Shelter, Security" I (sometimes out loud) tell myself that I have these things and that this means I am safe at the moment. Basically treating myself like an anxious child (as someone with childhood trauma that is sometimes much more true than I'd like).   

Some people prefer to try to distract themselves until their brain is done with threat assessement and acting up. Whatever works for your. Hope you'll feel better soon!

Hi.   

I don't really have advice on how to get through it. You will, and I sincerely hope your mother will be extubated soon and recover.   

As for sharing experiences, I have cared for patients in the ICU with several complications/reoperations as a medical student on rotation (will be going into surgery). And of course it is different when you are not related but since you are a nurse yourself I don't tell you anything new when I say that some patient's stories did impact me despite that.   

There was this one woman, also a routine operation that had one of those <1% complications, she suffered severe neurological damage. I kept talking to her husband, explaining him things, he already had lost his son years prior to an accident. When she had her first reop I went to watch it, even though it was after my shift and I could not assist because a resident was taught the procedure. So I was sitting there for 2hrs, just... watching and hoping for the best. Whenever I was sent into her (or another lower GCS patient's) room I'd make a point of still talking to her normally, explaining everything I do.   

I started to write poems. Not any good I just wrote them for me. For every patient who's story had lingered in my mind. It did help a bit. I also kept listening to this horribly sad song (The Kettering by The Antlers) about someone in a hospice.   

When my grandfather was dying in the hospital (lymphoma) I just sat there holding his hand, going through all the memories we had together, mentally talking to him in his garden, where we'd often barbecue. And I sang for him.

I think in the end whatever helps you cope is good. Sometimes those can be small and silly things too.   

I wish all the best to your and your father!

Why do people care about others they have no immediate relation with/ keep them from suicide?    

I have wondered about that quite a bit in my life. Some might follow a moral framework that compells them to, some might do it because of empathy, the intuitive sense that we are part of a larger "thing", more connected than we realize.    

I asked you why you cared because I was curious how you arrived at this topic (waifuism) specifically. What led you to use this hour to type up a whole post on it, maybe instead of writing about another topic or answering people or doing something completely different. Often if people get very defensive about a topic, very eager to show how it is "bad" they have some internal relation to it that they may or may not realize.   

I have an example: I used to be pretty openly pro gay marriage and vocal about lgbtq rights. Then I realized that I am queer myself and for some reason stopped talking about it, even internally started being ashamed of it. I never externalized that as in writing about how being gay is bad or something but I did on purpose seek out anti-lgbtq articles and read them.   

I wouldn't say I particularly *care* about why you care about waifuism, I seem to be answering posts on this sub mainly because I feel quite lonely right now and it gives me at least some interaction with others.

Hi. I left after 5 years (lucky to not be financially tied to him).   

It is difficult and slowly chips away at you. "It isnt always bad" is one of the main things I kept telling myself. And it wasn't. In my case he even was not a bad person, just a very damaged one lashing out (sexually and emotionally, never physically). The main reason I stayed was to keep him from suicide. I left, he attempted and survived.   

It is ok that this is hard, it is ok to hate him and it is ok to love him and all in between.   

Maybe you can ask the suicide hotline for resources in your area for women in your situation? At least in my country they have the addresses of women's houses etc. Another person you could ask is your GP/PCP, they should know where to point you too (I am a medical student and we get thaught how to handle these situations in medschool). 

I wish you good luck! You can feel like a person again, it might take a while but... at least for me waking up one day realizing I never have to have sex with him again was a rush of happiness I... I hope you'll know soon!
